newsitem.title: USA: RTRS-Zinc market heads for bull run - Rudolf Wolff.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Zinc market heads for bull run - Rudolf Wolff.

text.p: The zinc market is heading for a bull run, but producers and consumers should take advantage of any short-term corrective dip because they may be shortlived, analyst William Adams of Rudolf Wolff said.

"We are going into quite a strong bull market in a step fashion. If it will go up on trade and speculative fund buying, it will every now and again run into profit-taking and producer-type selling," Adams said. "It will come down and then go up again."

In a presentation to the American Zinc Association conference in Scottsdale earlier this week, Adams added that after absorbing extra Eastern metal, the market is now likely to have to readjust to falling East bloc exports.

Wolff forecast that Western mine production is set to hit 5.93 million tonnes this year, up from 5.68 million in 1996, while smelter production will increase to 5.7 million tonnes from 5.54 million in 1996.
Taking into account imports and U.S. government stockpile sales, a Western world deficit of 228,000 tonnes of zinc is expected this year, Wolff estimated.
"The demand profile looks strong, a deficit seems inevitable which will drawdown stocks further," Adams said.
Stocks will return to normal levels by the end of 1997. Total stocks are at 7.6 weeks' worth of consumption, while 6 weeks is considered critical, Adams said.

According to charts, after $1,240 per tonne has been cleared, $1,400 is a likely level for prices to reach during the next run up, but a downward correction to $1,080 or $1,090 per tonne was expected.
Adams said producers should take advantage of a short-term pullback by either selling outright futures, or selling nearby out of the market calls to receive the premium.

"And lot of the consumers, the galvanizers and steel companies, are probably underhedged as the price has moved up dramatically. The dips are likely to be well bought if the trade do come in and buy, but they will be competing with the funds who also will want to buy," Adams said.
Pullbacks might therefore be shortlived and not go as far down as people expected, he added.
